 Bulgarian Government Sets 2027 Minimum Wage at €660, Hourly Rate at €3.98
 Society | November 4, 2026, Wednesday // 10:03 
 Tweet 
 Share 
 Send to Kindle 
 Bulgaria ’s minimum monthly wage will rise to €660 from January 1, 2027, under a government decree published in the State Gazette, setting the minimum hourly rate at €3.98.
 The Council of Ministers adopted the decree on October 29, and it was published in the State Gazette on November 3. The new monthly rate applies to a full working month based on an eight-hour day and a five-day workweek.
 The increase amounts to €39.80, or 6.4%, compared with the current minimum wage of €620.20. Natalia Efremova, representing the Ministry of Labor and Social Policy, said the change would affect approximately 462,000 workers. During discussions on the proposal, she noted that the increase was higher than the annual inflation rate of 5.7% and was in line with the state budget’s capacity.
 The proposed amount was discussed on October 23 by the National Council for Tripartite Cooperation, but the meeting ended without agreement. All nationally representative employers’ organizations backed the government’s proposal, arguing that the 6.4% increase would fully compensate for inflation. The Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) also reported that employers supported the proposed figure, while trade unions opposed it.
 The Confederation of Labour "Podkrepa" said that, after personal social security contributions and income tax are deducted, workers would receive approximately €512 net. Union representatives argued that this amount does not provide a decent income and leaves Bulgarians earning the minimum wage at the bottom of the European Union in this respect. The Confederation of Independent Trade Unions in Bulgaria (CITUB), meanwhile, called for the minimum wage to be raised to €690.
 The 2027 increase is the first to be prepared under a new mechanism for setting the minimum wage. The system was introduced through amendments to the Labor Code adopted by Parliament in September, followed by the drafting of implementing regulations.
 Previously, the minimum wage was calculated using a formula linked to 50% of the average gross wage over a specified period. Under the new system, it must fall within a range determined by a lower and an upper threshold. The lower threshold cannot be below the previous year's minimum wage , while the upper one is calculated using four socio-economic indicators: the purchasing power of the minimum wage , including in relation to the cost of living; the overall level and distribution of wages; the rate of wage growth; and long-term labor productivity.
 Each of the four indicators accounts for 25% of the formula, with calculations based on official statistical data.
 Under the procedure, trade unions and employers must negotiate the minimum wage for the following year by May 15. The Council of Ministers is then required to set the specific amount by August 15, taking into account the discussions with social partners.
 The adequacy of the minimum wage will also be assessed every three years, using two reference points: 60% of the gross median wage and the cost of living. The government retains the authority to determine the final amount even if employers and trade unions fail to reach an agreement.
